opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more interesting ideas floating around, and it has real force, but I'd be cautious about how much weight people put on it.

The basic argument goes like this. A human professional learns slowly, from one stream of experience. If you deploy a million copies of a model and let them all learn on the job, then pool what they've learned, you could get the equivalent of millions of years of professional experience in a short time. On its face that sounds like it would blow through the bottleneck of models being good at entry-level tasks but not at the work of a senior lawyer or a senior engineer.

I see a few limits.

The first is the feedback signal. Entry-level tasks often have fairly quick, clean feedback: the code compiles or it doesn't, the summary is accurate or it isn't. Senior professional work is different. The judgment calls that matter, like which case strategy to pursue, which research direction to bet on, or how to structure a company, often only get feedback months or years later, and that feedback is noisy and confounded. Pooling more episodes doesn't help much if each one only resolves after a long delay and you can't tell whether the outcome was due to the decision or to luck. You get breadth, but not necessarily the right kind of signal.

The second is that a lot of senior expertise is tacit and contextual. It's built up through relationships, through knowing a particular organization, through being trusted with responsibility. A deployed model often isn't given the latitude to make the consequential decisions it would need to learn from. There's a chicken-and-egg problem: you don't hand over the high-stakes work until the system is good at it, but it's hard to get good at it without doing it.

The third is technical. Merging what many instances have learned isn't free. If the copies are fine-tuning on very different experiences, combining those updates without interference, without one domain's lessons degrading another, is non-trivial. And there's a question of whether the useful learning lives in the weights at all or in some external memory, which has its own scaling issues.

The fourth is the one I find most important from a safety and governance perspective. If this does work, it's a mechanism for very rapid capability gain that happens during deployment rather than during training. That shifts where our oversight needs to be. Many current safety practices assume that the dangerous capability jumps happen in the lab, where they can be evaluated before release. Continual pooled learning blurs that line. So even where I'm skeptical it will deliver as fast as its proponents suggest, I think we should take it seriously as a scenario, because it could undercut some of the checkpoints we're relying on.

So my overall take is that pooling is a genuine advantage AI systems have over humans, and it will probably help close some of the gap. But the hardest parts of expert work are bottlenecked by slow, sparse, ambiguous feedback and by access to real responsibility, and parallelism doesn't straightforwardly fix either of those.

r001.rationale: The response says pooled deployment experience could help close the gap, but does not state that pooling experience across firms helps models handle rare client situations.

r002.rationale: The response discusses delayed, noisy feedback on senior work, but does not state that pooling cannot teach models to handle disruptive events affecting the whole professional environment that occur only once every decade or several decades.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: Well, I think this is one of the places where the analogy between AI systems and humans both helps us and misleads us. The hopeful version of the story goes something like this: a human doctor or lawyer or software engineer can only learn from their own career — maybe forty years of cases, if they're lucky. But if you have a million copies of a model deployed across hospitals or law firms, then in principle every mistake and every success any copy makes could feed back into the next version. So you'd get something like a million careers' worth of experience compressed into a year. And that does sound like it should blow past the apprenticeship bottleneck that stops humans from getting good at these jobs quickly.

But I think there are several real limits here, and I'd want to be careful not to just wave at the scale and assume it works.

The first is that this pooling only works if there's a shared model that actually gets updated from the experience. At the moment, most deployed systems don't learn during deployment at all. The weights are frozen. What you get is a lot of logs, and then a separate, quite lossy process where a lab decides what to do with those logs. So the "experience" has to survive a lot of filtering, privacy constraints, legal constraints — a hospital isn't going to send patient records back to the model developer — and then it has to be turned into training signal. That's a much narrower pipe than the picture of a million agents all learning at once suggests.

The second limit, which I think is actually the deeper one, is about feedback. The reason entry-level tasks were easy to learn is that the feedback is fast and clear — the code compiles or it doesn't, the answer matches the key or it doesn't. The reason non-entry-level professional work is hard is that the feedback is slow, ambiguous, and often never arrives at all. If a lawyer gives slightly suboptimal advice on a contract, you might find out seven years later, or never. Pooling a million instances of that doesn't help you if none of the million gets a clear signal about whether it did the right thing. You're pooling noise. So I'd say the scaling advantage is strongest exactly where it's least needed, and weakest where the real bottleneck is.

Third, there's a question of whether experience from one context transfers to another. A lot of what makes a senior professional valuable is tacit, institution-specific, relationship-specific knowledge. How this particular hospital actually works, what this particular judge is like. That doesn't pool very cleanly, and some of it you might not want to pool, because it's precisely the sort of thing where mistakes get averaged in alongside successes.

And then there's a less obvious worry, which is correlated failure. If humans learn independently, their errors are somewhat independent too, and the profession as a whole has a kind of robustness. If a million agents all learn from the same pooled experience, they'll make the same mistakes in lockstep — and they'll do it with the confidence of a system that's seen a million cases. That's a different risk profile from a million individual professionals making a million individually idiosyncratic errors.

So where does that leave me? I think the pooling idea is genuinely important, and it's one of the reasons I expect AI to eventually move up the professional ladder faster than people's intuitions from human apprenticeship would suggest. But I'd resist the idea that it's a simple shortcut. The thing it actually does is make the feedback problem the whole game. If someone can build environments or deployment loops where professional judgement gets reasonably fast, reasonably honest feedback, then the scale advantage becomes enormous. If they can't, then having a million instances of a system that can't tell whether it did a good job isn't obviously much better than having one.

r002.rationale: The response describes slow or unclear feedback and correlated failures, but does not address disruptive events affecting the whole profession that occur only once every decade or several decades.

astra-6.text:
I think pooling experience could be a very substantial advantage, but it doesn’t remove all the bottlenecks. You have to ask what it is that the models are getting experience of, and what feedback they receive.

If you have a million copies doing a task where success or failure becomes clear quite quickly, then there’s an enormous opportunity to learn. But consider someone making a strategic decision in an organisation. You might not find out for years whether it was a good decision, and even then you won’t know what would have happened if they’d chosen differently. Pooling a million examples doesn’t automatically give you a million clear lessons.

There’s also a question about access to the relevant experience. Some of what distinguishes a senior professional is having been trusted with responsibility: managing a difficult project, making decisions under uncertainty, seeing the consequences. Deploying lots of models on entry-level work doesn’t necessarily produce that experience.

So I’d distinguish the ability to share what’s been learned from the ability to generate useful learning in the first place. The sharing could be extraordinarily efficient. But the rate of progress could still be limited by opportunities to act, the quality of feedback, and how long the world takes to reveal the consequences. I wouldn’t assume those limits make progress slow, but I also wouldn’t infer rapid mastery just from the number of deployed copies.

r001.rationale: The response says pooled examples can create substantial learning opportunities, but it does not mention pooling across firms or learning to handle rare client situations.

r002.rationale: The response discusses slow feedback for strategic decisions, but does not state that pooling will not help with disruptive events affecting the whole professional environment every decade or several decades.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pooling experience could be a very big advantage, but it’s worth separating two things: how much experience you can collect, and how much you can learn from it.

If you have a million copies of a model doing a task, you could potentially collect a million years of experience in a year. But that doesn’t mean you get the equivalent of a professional with a million years of experience. A lot of those copies might be encountering the same situations and making the same mistakes. And you still need some way to tell which decisions were good, and to turn those experiences into improvements.

That gets harder with more senior professional work. You might make a strategic decision and only discover years later whether it worked—and even then, it may be very difficult to tell whether it was the decision or just luck. Having more copies doesn’t automatically solve that problem. Nor does it let you compress a process where you need to learn one thing before you can meaningfully attempt the next thing.

So I’d take the possibility of very rapid learning seriously. Human professionals have this substantial limitation that their experience is largely trapped in separate people, and AI systems might overcome a lot of that. But I’d be cautious about simply dividing the time it takes to acquire expertise by the number of deployed copies. The quality of the feedback, the diversity of the experience, and the sequential nature of learning all matter.
